metadata.title: Startup websites that explain the product and drive action
metadata.description: Launch a startup website with a clear message, useful proof, a focused conversion path, and measurement from day one.

hero.title: Launch a startup site people understand quickly.
hero.summary: Turn a new product into a clear story, a focused website, and a launch you can measure.

problem.title: A new product is already hard to explain.
problem.introduction: The website should remove confusion, not add another layer of it. We watch for three common launch problems.

items.title: The message tries to say everything
items.description: A long list of features hides who the product is for and why anyone should care.

items.title: Claims arrive before proof
items.description: Big promises sound weak when the site does not show the product, the process, or honest limits.

items.title: The launch cannot be measured
items.description: Buttons, forms, and campaign visits go live without a simple event plan or a clear owner.

solution.title: Five things we settle before launch.
solution.introduction: The site starts small and specific. Every page and action earns its place.

items.title: Say who the product is for and what it changes.
items.description: We choose the main audience, the problem they feel, and the promise the product can support. Then we write it in plain language.
highlights: Lead with one audience and one problem
Remove internal terms and vague claims
Check the H1 and opening copy with new readers

items.title: Give every page one clear next step.
items.description: We match the primary action to the stage of the product. Visitors can join, book, apply, or learn more without guessing.
highlights: Keep supporting links useful and quiet
Test the full path on mobile and desktop

items.title: Show real proof without making things up.
items.description: We use the product, team, process, and honest answers already available. Missing customer proof stays missing until it is real.
highlights: Use verified team and company facts
Answer the questions that slow people down

items.title: Track the actions that matter.
items.description: We name the few events needed to understand the launch. Each event has a purpose, a trigger, and an owner.
highlights: Keep campaign attribution through the form
Test analytics in the production environment

items.title: Check the real launch, not only the preview.
items.description: We test the final domain, forms, metadata, analytics, robots, sitemap, and social preview before announcing the site.
highlights: Verify the production domain and indexability
Keep a rollback owner and launch record

method.title: A launch process that stays small.
method.introduction: The first version should answer the main questions well. More pages can follow when there is evidence they are needed.

steps.title: Choose the audience
steps.description: Write down who the site is for, what they need, and what the product can prove.

steps.title: Build the core path
steps.description: Finish the homepage, key proof, primary action, and required legal pages.

steps.title: Wire the measurement
steps.description: Add the event plan, attribution, form delivery, and consent rules.

steps.title: Test and launch
steps.description: Review the live domain, complete the checklist, and watch the first visits.

outcomes.title: What you have on launch day.

items.title: A clear product story
items.description: The homepage explains the audience, problem, product, and next step without a long pitch.

items.title: A working conversion path
items.description: The primary action works end to end and keeps the context needed for follow-up.

items.title: A useful launch baseline
items.description: The team can see what people viewed, what they tried, and what needs improvement.

faq.title: Common questions.
faq.introduction: Straight answers for teams trying to launch without turning the website into a second product.

items.question: How many pages does a startup need at launch?
items.answer: Only enough to explain the product, earn basic trust, and support the main action. Start with the core journey and add pages when real questions or search demand appear.

items.question: What if we do not have customer logos or testimonials?
items.answer: Do not invent them. Show the product, the team, the problem, and how the work happens. Add customer proof after you have permission to use it.

items.question: Should we publish before the product is ready?
items.answer: Yes, when the page has a real purpose such as collecting qualified interest. Be clear about what exists now and what happens after someone signs up.

items.question: Can the site grow after launch?
items.answer: Yes. The route structure, tokens, metadata helpers, and launch checklist are designed to support new pages without rebuilding the foundation.

cta.title: Launch the clearest useful version first.
cta.description: Give people enough to understand the product, trust the team, and take the next step. Learn from the launch before adding more.
